records.name: Snow Flea
records.diet: dead leaves and stems, fungal threads, pollen, and the pink algae that grow on old snow
records.shelter: Wet leaf litter, moss cushions, and the hollow gap between the snowpack and the ground in winter
records.preferredHabitat: Damp alpine turf, moss cushions and snowmelt litter, plus the surface of late-lying snow on warm days
records.fact: On a mild winter day snow fleas pour out onto the snow in their thousands, like somebody spilled pepper across the drift. Their blood is full of natural antifreeze, so they keep moving when everything else is frozen stiff.
records.role: The clean-up crew, and the reason last year's leaves do not simply pile up forever. Snow fleas shred dead stems and graze fungal threads into soil, and they keep at it all winter in the dark gap between the snowpack and the ground. Pipits, finches, chickadees, bluebirds, nutcrackers and toads all snap them up.

requirements.hint: A mat of litter under melting snow is enough to start.

records.name: Bighorn Sheep
records.diet: chiefly grasses and sedges, with forbs and woody browse in winter
records.shelter: Beds on rocky ledges and rugged escape terrain near cliffs
records.preferredHabitat: Open alpine turf directly beside steep, broken escape cliffs
records.fact: Rams charge each other and crash horns hard enough to be heard a mile off. Their skulls are double-layered to take the hit, and a lamb is climbing rock within a day of being born.
records.role: A cliff-edge grazer that crops turf on open slopes and never feeds further from broken rock than it can sprint. Mountain lions take adults and lambs, and eagles carry newborn lambs off the ledges.

requirements.hint: Good grazing is only half of it. A bighorn will not use a slope it cannot escape from, so put the turf right up against broken cliff, and a mineral lick nearby because sheep will travel a long way for salt.

records.name: Pika
records.diet: grasses, forbs, wildflowers and lichen, cut green and dried into winter haypiles
records.shelter: Cool gaps deep within talus and broken rock
records.preferredHabitat: Deep, stable talus with alpine flower turf right at its edge
records.fact: A pika spends its whole summer cutting flowers and grass and stacking them into little haystacks under the rocks, then eats its way through the pile in the dark under the snow.
records.role: A hamster-shaped cousin of rabbits that lives in the gaps inside talus and squeaks at anything that comes near. It overheats after an hour of warm sun, so it works at dawn and dusk, and it has already vanished from the lower, hotter rockslides, which makes it the mountain's early warning system. Weasels, martens, foxes, wolverines and eagles all hunt it.

requirements.hint: Deep talus to vanish into with flowers a short dash away, then a haypile. Without cured hay it cannot last the winter.

records.name: Yellow-bellied Marmot
records.diet: grasses, flowering plants and seeds, eaten hard through a short summer
records.shelter: Deep, many-chambered burrows dug beneath boulders, below the frost line
records.preferredHabitat: Open alpine turf broken by boulders, with diggable soil underneath
records.fact: A marmot sleeps for about eight months of the year and wakes up weighing half what it did when it went to bed.
records.role: A fat, sun-basking rodent that eats meadow plants flat out through a short summer and whistles from a boulder the moment a shadow crosses. Its old burrows become fox dens, bumble bee nests and toad hideouts, so a surprising amount of the mountain depends on its digging. Eagles, foxes, martens, wolverines and lions hunt it.

requirements.hint: Soil deep enough to dig, a boulder to dig under, and a lot of green within waddling distance. Do not go looking after early autumn, because it is underground until spring.

records.name: Snowshoe Hare
records.diet: green plants in summer; willow and juniper twigs, buds, bark and conifer needles in winter
records.shelter: Shallow 'forms' scraped under dense shrubs and low conifer branches
records.preferredHabitat: Dense krummholz, juniper and willow thickets at and just below treeline
records.fact: The hare changes colour by the calendar, not the weather. Shortening days flip its coat white whether the snow has turned up or not, so a warm autumn can leave a white hare sitting on brown ground.
records.role: A browsing hare of thick treeline cover with back feet like snowshoes that hold it up on top of drifts. It freezes rather than runs, so tangled low cover is everything to it, and willow twigs get it through the winter. Martens, foxes, eagles, wolverines and lions all hunt it.

requirements.hint: Low tangled cover it can freeze motionless inside, a scraped hollow under the krummholz to sit out the day, and willow to browse in winter. Open ground with a rock pile on it is the opposite of hare habitat. It eats snow instead of drinking.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Lepus americanus

records.name: White-tailed Ptarmigan
records.diet: buds, twigs, leaves, seeds and flowers; in winter almost entirely willow buds and twigs
records.shelter: Camouflaged ground scrapes among lichen-covered rock, and burrows dug into soft snow to roost
records.preferredHabitat: Alpine tundra above treeline year-round, dropping into sheltered willow basins in winter
records.fact: It grows feathers on its feet for winter, built-in snowshoes, and then dives into a snowdrift to sleep, because inside the drift it is far warmer than out in the wind.
records.role: A grouse that spends its entire life above the trees, mottled brown in summer and pure white in winter and so well hidden that people walk within a metre without seeing one. Willow buds are almost its whole winter diet. Eagles, foxes, weasels, martens and wolverines hunt it and its chicks.

requirements.hint: Willow is the whole winter for a ptarmigan, and a soft deep drift is its bedroom. It eats snow instead of drinking, and it has no use at all for a flower planter.

sources.name: All About Birds — White-tailed Ptarmigan life history

records.name: Alpine Butterfly
records.diet: stonecrop as a caterpillar, then nectar from stonecrop and daisies as an adult
records.shelter: No nest — the caterpillar develops fully inside the egg and overwinters there, hatching at snowmelt
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky open alpine and subalpine slopes where stonecrop grows between the stones
records.fact: Its wings are almost see-through, like waxed paper held up to the light, and the red spots are a warning. Birds that try one usually spit it straight back out.
records.role: A butterfly that flies in air most insects cannot manage. Its caterpillars eat stonecrop and absolutely nothing else, so the butterfly only lives where the stonecrop does, while the adults drift between meadow flowers for nectar. Pipits and bluebirds still catch a few.

requirements.hint: Nectar keeps the adults hanging around. Stonecrop is what keeps them for good. Plant flowers without the caterpillar's one food plant and all you get is visitors.

sources.name: Butterflies and Moths of North America — Parnassius smintheus

records.name: Alpine Moth
records.diet: flower nectar as an adult, drunk after dark; leaves and roots down in the lowlands as a caterpillar
records.shelter: Packed by the thousand into cracks under scree slabs, out of the sun and the wind
records.preferredHabitat: High rockslides beside flower turf — but only in summer; it spends the rest of the year far below
records.fact: Every summer millions of these moths fly up out of the lowlands and hide in the rock on the highest peaks. They are so fatty that a bear will spend all day flipping stones to eat them, and can put away forty thousand moths in a single day.
records.role: The mountain's fuel delivery. The moths fatten on lowland flowers, then migrate hundreds of kilometres uphill to sit out the summer in the cold rock, and every one arrives as a little parcel of fat richer than anything else growing up here. Bears, birds and just about everything that hunts a rockslide feeds on them. At night they come out to drink nectar and pollinate high-country flowers; by dawn they are back under the slabs. Break up the loose rock and the whole larder goes with it.
eatsOther: leaves and roots as a caterpillar

requirements.hint: Flowers to drink from at night and loose slabs to hide under by day. It only shows up in high summer — the rest of the year it is a caterpillar a long way downhill.

sources.name: USGS Northern Rocky Mountain Science Center — Army Cutworm Moth Aggregation Sites

records.name: Rock Squirrel
records.diet: seeds, berries and green shoots, plus underground fungi, insects and the occasional egg
records.shelter: A burrow driven in under a boulder or a fallen log, with a grass-lined sleeping chamber at the far end
records.preferredHabitat: Sunny rocky slopes, talus edges and open dwarf-pine ground at and above the tree line
records.fact: Everyone calls it a giant chipmunk, but look at its face — no stripes on the cheeks. And it does not just nap through winter: it cools until its body is barely above freezing and its heart slows to a few beats a minute.
records.role: A stripe-backed seed machine that spends the short summer eating itself round, then vanishes underground for half the year. It buries seeds all over the slope and forgets enough of them to replant it, and it digs up and eats underground fungi, so the spores ride through its gut and get planted somewhere new. Ermines, martens, lynx and eagles all hunt it, and the tunnels it abandons become shelter for toads and beetles.

requirements.hint: It is only above ground for half the year, so look for it in the warm months. Seed-heavy flowers to fatten on, rock to duck into, and diggable ground under a boulder for the long sleep.

sources.name: Montana Field Guide — Golden-mantled Ground Squirrel

records.name: Nutcracker
records.diet: whitebark and limber pine seeds cached by the thousand, plus insects and small animals
records.shelter: Cup nest in a conifer, sited near the winter seed caches
records.preferredHabitat: Treeline conifer forest and krummholz within reach of pine-seed sources
records.fact: One bird buries tens of thousands of pine seeds in a single autumn and can still find them months later under snow, navigating by rocks and logs it has memorised like landmarks on a map.
records.role: A crow-family bird with a deal running with the whitebark pine. The cones never open by themselves, so nearly every young whitebark on the mountain grew from a seed this bird buried and never came back for. It carries seeds in a pouch under its tongue, breeds in late winter off its hoard, and takes insects and small animals besides. Martens and eagles catch it.

requirements.hint: It needs a seed bank it can find again under the snow. Build the caches, and the pines it forgets to dig up become next year's forest.

sources.name: All About Birds — Clark's Nutcracker life history

records.name: Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch
records.diet: tiny alpine plant seeds and insects, often gleaned off the surface of snowfields
records.shelter: Bulky cup of moss and grass wedged deep into a cliff crack or a hole in talus
records.preferredHabitat: Above treeline: talus, scree, cliff faces and the edges of permanent snow
records.fact: It nests higher than almost any other songbird here, jammed into cracks in cliffs and rockslides where nothing else will build at all.
records.role: A pink-brown finch that hops across snowfields picking up wind-blown seeds and insects the cold has knocked flat. It can only breed where the rock has real cracks in it, so cliffs matter to it even more than food does. Eagles and ermines take it.

requirements.hint: Rock with cracks in it, not a heap of stones. A rosy-finch nests inside the cliff, feeds out across the scree, and drinks meltwater.

sources.name: All About Birds — Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch life history

records.name: Pipit
records.diet: mostly insects, springtails, spiders and their larvae, plus some seeds
records.shelter: Ground nest of grass tucked into the turf beside a rock or a tussock
records.preferredHabitat: Open alpine turf and fellfield, especially along the edges of melting snow
records.fact: Wind sweeps insects up off the lowlands and dumps them on the snowfields, chilled and helpless. The pipit walks the edge of the melting snow eating a meal the weather delivered uphill.
records.role: A slim brown ground-walker that bobs its tail non-stop as it hunts across open turf. It nests in a scrape tucked beside a rock and feeds heavily on that stranded insect fallout, one of the strangest free lunches in the mountains. Foxes and ermines take it and its ground nests.

requirements.hint: Open turf to walk and nest in, and a lingering snowbank with a dark line of debris along its edge. That stripe is the dinner table.

sources.name: Birds of the World — American Pipit food habits

records.name: Boreal Toad
records.diet: beetles, ants, flies, springtails and other invertebrates; tadpoles graze algae
records.shelter: Rodent burrows, rock chambers and damp cover above the breeding pools
records.preferredHabitat: Subalpine and alpine wet meadows with shallow, sun-warmed, fish-free breeding pools
records.fact: It spends September to May underground, then comes out and breeds in pools that were solid ice a few weeks earlier.
records.role: The only toad living this high. Adults eat insects by the thousand and the tadpoles graze algae in shallow, sun-warmed pools, and almost nothing eats them because their skin tastes foul. What actually threatens this toad is a skin fungus and trout stocked into lakes that never had fish.

requirements.hint: Shallow warm pools to breed in and a burrow to spend the other eight months of the year in. Keep the pools fishless, because stocked trout are the single biggest reason high-country amphibians disappear.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Anaxyrus boreas
NPS Rocky Mountain NP — Where do boreal toads spend the winter?
Colorado Parks and Wildlife — Boreal Toad

records.name: White-throated Swift
records.diet: flying insects only — moths, beetles, flies and drifting swarms of ants, all taken in mid-air
records.shelter: A cup of feathers glued with its own spit into a narrow crack in a cliff face
records.preferredHabitat: Sheer cliffs and broken crags with a lot of open air in front of them to hunt in
records.fact: It does everything in the air. It eats in the air, drinks in the air, and pairs mate in mid-air — locking together and tumbling hundreds of feet down the cliff face before they let go.
records.role: A blade-shaped bird that lives in the sky above the mountain, hoovering up moths, beetles and whatever else the wind lifts, at speeds that make it one of the fastest birds alive in level flight. Its feet only cling, never perch, so it has to fold itself into a crack in a cliff at night, and it sticks the nest in place with its own saliva. Because it eats only what is flying, a swift working the ridge is proof the insect life below has come back. Almost nothing is quick enough to catch one.

requirements.hint: A narrow crack in a cliff to sleep in and a lot of open air in front of it. It never lands to feed and it drinks on the wing, so any pool it can skim will do.

records.name: Mountain Chickadee
records.diet: insects, spiders and bark-beetle larvae in summer; cached conifer seeds in fall and winter
records.shelter: Existing cavities in dead conifers — old woodpecker holes, or soft rotten wood it can enlarge
records.preferredHabitat: Treeline conifer forest of fir and whitebark pine with standing dead trees
records.fact: It hides thousands of seeds one at a time and remembers where they are. The part of its brain that does the remembering actually grows bigger in autumn.
records.role: The small busy bird that seems to be everywhere in the last trees, hanging upside down off twigs after insects and beetle grubs and switching to hidden seeds in winter. It can only nest where the wood has already gone soft, so dead trees are not mess, they are the nursery. Weasels, foxes and martens take it.

requirements.hint: Dead trees are the point. A beetle-killed snag is both the chickadee's larder and the only wood soft enough for it to hollow out. The whitebark pines come from it's forgotten seeds.

sources.name: All About Birds — Mountain Chickadee life history

records.name: Lynx
records.diet: snowshoe hares above all — sometimes almost nothing else — plus ptarmigan, ground squirrels and young marmots
records.shelter: A hollow under boulders, roots or deadfall, often a burrow something else started and it widened
records.preferredHabitat: High snowy country with thickets of dwarf conifer where hares can hide and lynx can wait for them
records.fact: A lynx weighs about as much as a border collie, but its paws are as wide as a mountain lion's. They spread as it steps, so it walks on top of snow a fox would sink straight through.
records.role: The mountain's hare specialist, and almost nothing else will do. When hares are everywhere, lynx are everywhere; when the hares crash a few years later, the lynx crash right behind them, and the whole thing swings back and forth on roughly a ten-year beat. It hunts by sitting perfectly still in the thickets and letting the hare come to it, so low tangled cover matters more to it than open ground. It rarely digs, moving instead into a hollow under rock that somebody else opened up. Eagles take its kittens.

requirements.hint: No hares, no it — it really is that simple. Get the dwarf-pine thickets back so hares have somewhere to hide, and it will move into a hollow under the rocks that something else dug.

records.name: Pine Marten
records.diet: voles, red squirrels, pikas, hares, birds, eggs, insects and berries
records.shelter: Dens in hollow logs, tree cavities and rock crevices, usually under deep snow
records.preferredHabitat: Structurally complex treeline forest with big trees, dead wood and rock
records.fact: In winter a marten hunts inside the snowpack, in the hollow spaces between the drifts and the ground, where nothing else its size can follow it.
records.role: A cat-sized weasel equally at home in the treetops and the snow tunnels, hunting voles, pikas, young hares and birds, with berries in late summer. Structure is what it needs above everything else, so a cleared slope empties of martens even while the prey is still there. Eagles catch it.

requirements.hint: You cannot build marten habitat out of rocks and flowers. It needs a stand of real trees, dead wood on the ground, and hares and they already living there.

sources.name: Alaska Department of Fish and Game — American marten

records.name: Ermine
records.diet: small rodents, especially voles; also young pikas, birds, eggs and insects
records.shelter: Dens taken over from its prey — rodent burrows and rock crevices, relined with the previous owner's fur
records.preferredHabitat: Talus and heath edges beside turf with dense rodent prey, used all year round
records.fact: An ermine turns pure white in winter except for the black tip of its tail, and it is narrow enough to chase a vole down the vole's own tunnel.
records.role: A weasel shaped like a furry pencil, living mostly on voles and mice and taking young pikas, nestlings and eggs besides. It builds nothing. It moves into the burrow of whatever it has just eaten and lines the nest with the previous owner's fur. It is here in every season, not only in the snow. Foxes, martens and eagles kill it in turn.

requirements.hint: It moves into a burrow it has just emptied, so bring the small rodents back first.

sources.name: Idaho Fish and Game species catalog — ermine

records.name: Golden Eagle
records.diet: marmots, hares, ground squirrels, ptarmigan and other birds, plus carrion
records.shelter: Huge stick eyries built on sheer cliff ledges and reused for decades
records.preferredHabitat: Open, high country with big cliffs to nest on and plenty of medium-sized prey
records.fact: A hunting golden eagle drops out of the sky at over 240 kilometres an hour, and its eyesight is sharp enough to pick a marmot out of a boulder field from a kilometre up.
records.role: The hunter that owns the air up here, taking marmots, hares and ptarmigan in long stooping dives and killing smaller predators outright when it gets the chance. It takes newborn lambs, kids and fox cubs, but not adult sheep or goats. Its huge stick eyrie on a cliff ledge gets added to and reused for decades. Adults have nothing above them.

requirements.hint: Eagles come last, when the mountain is properly alive again. They need a real cliff for the eyrie and open ground below with plenty moving on it.

sources.name: All About Birds — Golden Eagle life history
Birds of the World — Golden Eagle food habits

records.name: Purple Sea Urchin
records.diet: living kelp and surfgrass, drift kelp, and encrusting coralline algae
records.shelter: Pits it grinds into the rock itself with its teeth and spines
records.preferredHabitat: Wave-exposed low intertidal and shallow subtidal rock near kelp
records.fact: A purple urchin chews a pit into solid rock with five teeth and then sits in it for years. On some reefs the urchins wear away more stone than the waves do.
records.role: The grazer at the middle of this coast's most famous story. Fed on scraps of drift kelp and kept in check by otters, urchins are just one more part of a healthy forest. Take the predators away and they march up the rock, mow the kelp to bare stone, and leave an urchin barren behind them.

requirements.hint: Kelp first — an urchin has to have something to eat. Then think hard about what is going to eat the urchins.

records.name: Anchovy
records.diet: plankton — copepods, diatoms and larvae — strained from the water or picked one at a time
records.shelter: The school itself; open nearshore water, with kelp and surfgrass edges as nursery cover
records.preferredHabitat: Cool, plankton-rich nearshore water over the shelf
records.fact: An anchovy eats two ways: it snaps at big prey one bite at a time, or just opens its mouth and swims, straining the sea like a living net.
records.role: Anchovies travel in silver schools so thick they turn the water dark from below. Almost everything that hunts here takes them at some point — pelicans, seals, dolphins, gulls — so when the anchovies fail, the whole coast goes hungry at once.

requirements.hint: Cold water rising from the deep grows the plankton they eat, and quiet shallows give the schools somewhere to spawn.

records.name: Beach Hopper
records.diet: decaying kelp and other stranded seaweed in the wrack line
records.shelter: Burrows dug in damp sand high on the beach, and the damp underside of drift kelp and driftwood
records.preferredHabitat: Gently sloping sandy beach with an undisturbed wrack line
records.fact: Beach hoppers spend all day sealed inside a burrow in dry sand, then pour out after dark to shred the seaweed the tide left behind. Step near one and it fires itself into the air like a flicked pebble.
records.role: The engine room of the beach. Hoppers chew stranded kelp down into crumbs and nutrients, and in doing so they turn dead seaweed into bird food — which is the entire reason plovers, sanderlings and gulls patrol the tide line. Rake the wrack away and this link vanishes overnight.

requirements.hint: Leave the seaweed where the tide drops it. That is the whole meal.

sources.name: California Conservation Genomics Project — Megalorchestia californiana

records.name: Hermit Crab
records.diet: algae, detritus, and scavenged carrion
records.shelter: Borrowed empty snail shells
records.preferredHabitat: Tidepools and low rock benches with a supply of empty snail shells
records.fact: Hermit crabs queue up by size and swap houses in a chain: the biggest one moves into the new shell, the next takes the house it left, and so on all the way down the line until the smallest crab gets an upgrade.
records.role: A tidepool tidier that grazes algae and cleans up dead things — and one of the shore's great recyclers, since every shell it wears is the leftover of a snail. What limits hermit crabs is almost never food. It is houses.

requirements.hint: A pool is not enough. Leave a supply of empty snail shells, or there is nothing to move into.

records.name: Bat Star
records.diet: algae, detritus, and dead plants and animals
records.shelter: Rocky rubble bottoms, surfgrass beds and kelp holdfasts
records.preferredHabitat: Shallow rocky and rubble bottom with surfgrass or kelp
records.fact: A bat star eats by pushing its stomach out through its mouth and spreading it over its meal, digesting food outside its own body. It also refuses to stick to five arms — four to nine is perfectly normal.
records.role: The cleanup crew of the shallows. It slides over the seafloor digesting algae, scraps and dead animals exactly where they lie, doing the same job a mushroom or an earthworm does on land — just wetter, and with more arms.

requirements.hint: Broken rock and rubble with surfgrass streaming over it. This is a rocky-bottom animal, not an eelgrass one.

records.name: Mussel
records.diet: plankton filtered from seawater
records.shelter: Dense beds anchored to wave-washed rock by byssal threads
records.preferredHabitat: Exposed rocky shore with clean, constantly moving water
records.fact: A mussel glues itself to the rock with threads it spins out of its own foot — and if it does not like where it landed, it cuts them, crawls a little way, and glues itself down again.
records.role: A shellfish that builds its own reef. The beds pile up thick enough that hundreds of smaller animals live in the gaps between shells, and half this shore's hunters — sea stars, oystercatchers, turnstones, otters — are really just here for the mussels.

requirements.hint: A filter feeder needs water that keeps moving. Give it surge-washed rock rather than a still pool, and barnacle crust for the baby they to settle on.

records.name: Gray Whale
records.diet: bottom-living amphipods and swarming mysid shrimp, sifted through baleen
records.shelter: Open ocean; passes close inshore along a healthy coast
records.preferredHabitat: Nearshore water with soft-bottom amphipod beds and mysid swarms at the kelp edge
records.fact: Gray whales roll onto one side and vacuum the seafloor, straining out shrimp-like amphipods and leaving long muddy plumes trailing behind them — and they do it at the end of a swim of up to 14,000 miles.
records.role: A baleen whale that feeds off the bottom rather than skimming the surface, so a whale that lingers offshore is really a report on the seabed and the kelp edge below it. Adults are far too big to be hunted here; the calves travelling with them in spring are not, and orcas know it.

requirements.hint: Give this one deep water and a seabed thick with tiny shrimp-like amphipods. Tidepools and dune plantings will never bring a whale in.

sources.name: Hildebrand et al. 2024, Sci Rep — urchin/kelp cascade and gray whale foraging

records.name: Brant Goose
records.diet: eelgrass, plus sea lettuce and other green algae
records.shelter: Open shoreline, sandbars and shallow bays
records.preferredHabitat: Shallow coastal bays with eelgrass beds
records.fact: Brant fly thousands of miles to eat basically one thing: eelgrass. Lose the eelgrass in a bay and the geese are gone within a season or two, no matter how nice the rest of it looks.
records.role: A small sea goose that grazes eelgrass and green algae in shallow bays and almost nothing else. Because it is so fussy, a bay full of brant is a bay with healthy seagrass — they are a living gauge of the meadow below them.

requirements.hint: Eelgrass to graze, and a quiet sandbar to stand on while the tide is too high to feed.

records.name: Shore Crab
records.diet: mostly algae and drift kelp, plus detritus, worms, snails and carrion
records.shelter: Crevices in splash-zone rock
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky intertidal and splash zone, often out of the water altogether
records.fact: The shore crab spends more than half its life out of the sea, breathing air on dry rock, and only nips back to a pool now and then to wet its gills.
records.role: The busiest scavenger on the highest rocks, scraping surfaces clean of algae and hauling away anything that dies. It is also breakfast for gulls, oystercatchers and turnstones, and one of the very first animals to reappear on a shore that is coming back to life.

requirements.hint: Barely any water. High rock, deep cracks to wedge into, and one pool nearby to duck into when it needs a drink.

records.name: Gull
records.diet: fish, crabs, mussels, sea stars and carrion
records.shelter: Ground scrapes on offshore rocks and islands, tucked beside driftwood, rock or low coastal scrub
records.preferredHabitat: Any shoreline with food to scavenge or catch
records.fact: A gull that finds a mussel it cannot open carries it high into the air and drops it onto rock — and it remembers which rock cracks shells best, coming back to the same one all season.
records.role: A bold, clever generalist that scavenges carrion and hunts crabs, shellfish, anchovies and even sea stars, tying dozens of small animals to the top of the food web. Nothing on this shore hunts a grown gull, which is exactly why it can afford to be so cheeky.

requirements.hint: Open beach to patrol, low scrub to nest beside, and one hard flat rock to bomb shellfish onto.

records.name: Sanderling
records.diet: beach hoppers, mole crabs, amphipods, worms and small molluscs
records.shelter: Open beach above the surf line
records.preferredHabitat: The wet swash zone of an open sandy beach
records.fact: Sanderlings spend the whole day sprinting at the sea and running away from it, chasing each wave out to grab whatever it uncovered and fleeing the next one before it buries them.
records.role: A specialist of the sliding strip of water at the sea's edge, feeding on the small crustaceans the surf keeps turning over. Its flocks live or die on how much life the wrack line produces, so a beach that is groomed clean is a beach without sanderlings.

requirements.hint: The wet strip where the waves run out, with open sand behind it. Do not plant anything here — this bird feeds where the water slides.

records.name: Snowy Plover
records.diet: beach invertebrates: beach hoppers, kelp flies and their larvae, small crustaceans and molluscs
records.shelter: A shallow scrape on open sand, sometimes lined with shell fragments; chicks shelter beside driftwood and wrack
records.preferredHabitat: Wide, flat, sparsely vegetated open sand above the tide line
records.fact: A snowy plover's entire nest is a dent in bare sand lined with a few shell chips. The chicks run within hours of hatching, and freeze flat as pebbles the moment a shadow crosses them.
records.role: A threatened beach nester that feeds on tiny invertebrates along the sand and the wrack. It will not nest where it cannot see a predator coming, which makes it one of the very few animals here that thick planting drives away rather than attracts — the kindest thing you can build it is emptiness nobody walks through.

requirements.hint: No water, no planting. Bare open sand, a roped-off patch where nobody treads, and driftwood for the chicks to hide beside.

records.name: Black Turnstone
records.diet: barnacles, limpets, small mussels, hermit crabs and other rocky-shore invertebrates
records.shelter: Rocky shoreline; tight flocks on raised rock at high tide
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky intertidal shores with barnacle and limpet crusts
records.fact: A turnstone does exactly what its name promises — flips over stones, shells and clumps of seaweed to snatch whatever is hiding underneath — and hammers barnacles open with a stubby bill shaped like a chisel.
records.role: A rocky-shore forager that pries barnacles and limpets loose and turns over wrack for hidden prey. It also needs somewhere safe to sit out high tide, when every feeding rock it owns is underwater. Take away the roosts and the shore loses its turnstones even with the food untouched.

requirements.hint: Barnacle-crusted rock to hammer at when the tide is out, and a high dry rock to stand on when it is not.

records.name: Crow
records.diet: crabs, shellfish, eggs, insects, fruit and whatever the tide leaves behind
records.shelter: A bulky stick nest high in a shore pine, reused and repaired year after year
records.preferredHabitat: The strip where the beach meets the trees, with a clear view of the tideline
records.fact: Crows work out that a shell will break if you drop it on rock, and they pick their spot — one that has learned the trick will carry a clam up, drop it, and adjust its height until the shell cracks. They also remember faces for years.
records.role: The sharpest bird on the shore. It patrols the tideline for anything stranded, cracks open what it can't bite through, and follows the gulls and the otters to see what they turn up.

requirements.hint: A tall tree back from the beach to nest in, and a wrack line worth patrolling. It will find everything else on its own.

records.name: Sea Star
records.diet: mussels above all, plus barnacles, limpets, chitons, snails and small urchins
records.shelter: Damp surge channels and rock crevices at the lower edge of the mussel bed
records.preferredHabitat: Wave-washed rocky intertidal with mussel beds above and surge below
records.fact: This is the animal the word 'keystone' was invented for. Take the sea stars off a shore and within a couple of years the mussels spread down over everything else — which is precisely what happened when a wasting disease melted these stars by the million along thousands of miles of coast.
records.role: The rocky shore's most famous predator. Working upward from the low zone and eating mussels as it goes, it decides where the mussel bed stops, and that leaves bare space on the rock for barnacles, algae, anemones and dozens of other species. Remove it and the mussels simply take everything.

requirements.hint: Build the mussel bed first. It lives along the bed's bottom edge, and that edge only exists because something is holding it there.

sources.name: MARINe (UC Santa Cruz) — Pisaster and sea star wasting disease

records.name: Anemone
records.diet: crabs, detached mussels and small fish stung by its tentacles
records.shelter: The walls and floors of surge-flushed pools, characteristically just below the mussel beds
records.preferredHabitat: Clear, sunlit, surge-fed pools in the low zone
records.fact: That glowing green comes from algae living inside the anemone's own body, making sugar out of sunlight and handing it over like rent. An anemone stuck in the shade goes pale and goes hungry.
records.role: A sit-still hunter that waits below the mussel beds and catches whatever the surf knocks loose from above, while farming its own private algae for extra meals. Half its food arrives by accident, falling out of the rocks overhead.

requirements.hint: A sunlit pool with surge running through it, sitting below a mussel bed. Dinner falls in from upstairs.

sources.name: Monterey Bay Aquarium — Giant green anemone

records.name: Puffin
records.diet: small fish carried crosswise in its beak, plus shrimp and other small swimmers
records.shelter: A burrow dug a metre back into the turf on top of a sea cliff
records.preferredHabitat: Grassy clifftops above deep water, with soil soft enough to dig
records.fact: A puffin can hold a dozen fish crosswise in its beak at once without dropping any — backward-pointing spines on its tongue and the roof of its mouth pin each one while it catches the next.
records.role: A small seabird that lives almost its whole life out on the water and only comes ashore to nest, digging a burrow into the clifftop turf. Its beak only turns bright orange for the breeding season, then dulls again for winter.

requirements.hint: Soft turf on top of a cliff to dig a burrow into, and deep water below it full of small fish.

records.name: Brown Pelican
records.diet: small schooling fish, especially northern anchovy
records.shelter: Nests only on undisturbed offshore islands; loafs on sandbars and rocks
records.preferredHabitat: Anchovy-rich nearshore water within reach of an island colony
records.fact: A brown pelican dives from sixty feet up and hits the water hard enough to stun fish — and it twists its body left just before impact so the blow does not break its neck.
records.role: A plunge-diving anchovy hunter whose comeback after pesticide poisoning is one of the great conservation rescues. It nests only on islands offshore, never on the mainland beach, and its colonies fail outright in years when the anchovy schools do not show — so a nesting pelican is a statement about the fish, not the sand.

requirements.hint: An island the tide and the footpaths cannot reach, sandbars to loaf on, and it schools in the water offshore.

records.name: Sea Otter
records.diet: sea urchins above all, plus mussels, crabs and sea stars
records.shelter: Rafts wrapped in living surface kelp canopy, in coves calm enough to groom in
records.preferredHabitat: Kelp forest and rocky shore with abundant shellfish and calm rafting water
records.fact: A sea otter has no blubber at all — just the thickest fur on Earth, about a million hairs in a patch the size of a postage stamp — so it spends hours a day combing air into its coat, and wraps itself in kelp so it does not drift away while it sleeps.
records.role: The animal this whole coast hangs on. By eating urchins it stops them mowing the kelp down to bare rock, so the forest and everything sheltering in it survives. Remove the otter and the urchins multiply, the kelp goes, and what is left is a barren. Note what it rafts in: living canopy, not dead wrack on the beach.

requirements.hint: Living kelp forest to wrap up in, calm water to groom in, and urchins and shellfish to eat. Dead kelp on the sand is no use to an otter.

records.name: Harbor Seal
records.diet: fish, especially anchovy and flatfish, plus squid, octopus and crustaceans
records.shelter: Undisturbed low-tide rocks and sandbars used as haul-outs for resting and pupping
records.preferredHabitat: Calm, clean water beside a haul-out nobody walks up to
records.fact: Harbor seals can sleep at sea, hanging upright just below the surface like bottles and bobbing up for a breath without properly waking.
records.role: A patient, curious hunter that eats whatever fish is easiest to catch that week. Everything it does on land happens on a haul-out: resting, moulting, giving birth. Walk up to one once and the seals stop using it. Nothing on this shore hunts an adult seal — but something out in the deep water does.

requirements.hint: Deep water to fish in and quiet rocks to haul out on, with room around them. A seal haul-out is not a bird nesting closure — build the right thing.

records.name: Desert Termite
records.diet: dead grass, fallen leaves, dry dung and the weathered outsides of dead wood
records.shelter: Tunnels and chambers underground, plus mud sheeting built over whatever it is eating
records.preferredHabitat: Soil beneath shrubs and grasses where dead plant litter collects
records.fact: These termites plaster a thin mud roof over a dead stem and eat underneath it, so they can feed in full sun without ever touching the dry air.
records.role: The animal that actually recycles this desert. There is too little water here for litter to rot the way it does in a forest, so termites eat almost all of it instead, carrying the nitrogen and carbon back underground and leaving tunnels that let rain soak in rather than run off. On swarm nights, everything with a beak or a sting comes to the feast.

requirements.hint: Bury a little dead wood and they will find it — dead wood is the desert’s pantry.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service — Physical and chemical alteration of soil by two subterranean termite species in a desert grassland

records.name: Jackrabbit
records.diet: grasses, wildflowers, cactus pads, and the twigs and bark of desert shrubs
records.shelter: A shallow shaded scrape under a shrub; it never digs a burrow
records.preferredHabitat: Open flats with scattered shrubs and room to run
records.fact: Those enormous ears are radiators — a jackrabbit lies dead still in the shade and pours its body heat straight out through the blood vessels inside them.
records.role: The biggest everyday plant-eater here, and the meal at the centre of everyone else's day. Its babies are born furred and open-eyed in a shallow scrape, because a jackrabbit owns no burrow and never will — it bets everything on ears, speed and knowing where the shade is.

requirements.hint: Grass to graze, shrubs to browse and a shaded scrape to lie in. Skip the water — it drinks from the plants.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Lepus californicus

records.name: Kangaroo Rat
records.diet: seeds, carried home in fur-lined cheek pouches and buried in underground larders
records.shelter: Shallow burrows under shrubs and soil mounds, plugged with sand every dawn
records.preferredHabitat: Loose soil under seed-bearing shrubs and mesquite
records.fact: A kangaroo rat never drinks — it manufactures all the water it needs out of dry seeds — and it can leap sideways almost two metres to dodge a striking snake.
records.role: The desert's accidental gardener. It buries seeds all over its patch and forgets enough of them that those are the plants that come up next spring. Its tunnels are the starting point for everything that cannot dig well: kit foxes widen them into dens, and half the burrows in the biome began as its work. Nearly every predator here eats it.

requirements.hint: Seed plants and soft diggable soil, especially the loose mounds heaped round a shrub's base. Build no water at all — this one may never take a drink in its life.

records.name: Desert Tortoise
records.diet: native grasses, spring wildflowers, and cactus pads and fruit
records.shelter: Caliche caves, rock crevices and dens under boulders on rocky slopes
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky slopes with native grasses and wildflowers
records.fact: A desert tortoise can live 80 years and spends about 95 of every 100 days of it underground — and it carries a bladder of stored water it can live off for a year if the rains fail.
records.role: A slow, long-lived grazer that also happens to be the landlord. The dens it hollows out get used for years afterwards by owls, snakes, lizards, rodents and insects that could never dig anything like them, so saving one tortoise quietly saves a dozen other animals. Grown tortoises are nearly untouchable; it is the hatchlings, soft-shelled for years, that ravens and coyotes take.

requirements.hint: A caliche den on a rocky slope, with grass and wildflowers to graze in front of it. It drinks only when rain puddles, and can wait a whole year for that.

sources.name: Desert Tortoise Council — Biology of Desert Tortoises

records.name: Cactus Bee
records.diet: pollen and nectar from prickly pear and cholla flowers
records.shelter: A vertical nest shaft dug in bare, loose ground, often with a little mud chimney over the door
records.preferredHabitat: Blooming prickly pear and cholla beside open, undisturbed soil
records.fact: Every female digs her own nest and stocks it herself — but thousands of these single mothers dig side by side in the same patch of bare ground, so the whole ground hums.
records.role: The bee that makes cactus fruit happen. No bee visits means no fruit set, and no fruit means no midsummer water for the squirrels, birds and rodents that live on it. She needs soft, undisturbed bare soil to dig in, which is exactly what hooves and tyres destroy first.

requirements.hint: Cactus flowers to work and a patch of loose, unpacked ground to dig in. Trampled hardpan is useless to her.

sources.name: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum — Cactus Bee nesting sites

records.name: Desert Hummingbird
records.diet: nectar from chuparosa, ocotillo and creosote flowers, plus small insects and spiders
records.shelter: A thimble-sized cup of plant down and spider silk in a low shrub
records.preferredHabitat: Washes and flats with shrubs that flower in winter and spring
records.fact: The male dives past the female at full speed and shrieks — except the shriek comes from his tail feathers, not his throat — while flaring a violet moustache of feathers out sideways.
records.role: A nectar-drinker that chases the bloom, arriving with the winter flowers of chuparosa and moving on as the desert dries out. It never needs to find water, and on the hardest days it switches itself almost off, dropping into a torpor so deep it feels cold to the touch.

requirements.hint: Real flowers beat a feeder every time: chuparosa blooms right through the desert winter, and ocotillo takes over in spring.

sources.name: Sonoran Joint Venture — Costa's Hummingbird species account
Cornell Lab All About Birds — Costa's Hummingbird Life History

records.name: Quail
records.diet: seeds, green leaves and cactus fruit — and, for the first weeks of life only, insects
records.shelter: A ground nest tucked under a shrub; the covey roosts up inside thorny cover at night
records.preferredHabitat: Thorny thickets along washes, within walking distance of water
records.fact: One male stands sentry on a high branch with that comma of feathers bobbing on his forehead while the rest of the covey feeds below, and when he calls the alarm the whole group runs — quail would nearly always rather sprint than fly.
records.role: A sociable ground bird living on seeds and greens, with the chicks fattened on insects for their first few weeks. Unlike almost everything else here it genuinely has to drink, so coveys walk the same path to the same water every summer day. Coyotes and hawks take adults; ravens and roadrunners take eggs and chicks.

requirements.hint: Thorny thickets to roost in and seeds to eat — and unlike most of this desert, water it can actually drink.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Gambel's Quail Life History

records.name: Cactus Woodpecker
records.diet: insects, cactus fruit and mistletoe berries
records.shelter: Cavities it chisels out of living saguaros
records.preferredHabitat: Saguaro stands with mesquite and washes nearby
records.fact: It chisels a hole into a living cactus and then waits months, doing nothing, while the plant seals the raw walls with hard scar tissue — only then will it move in.
records.role: The only animal here that can build a home from scratch, and half the biome lives in its leftovers: elf owls, kestrels, flycatchers and wild bees all move into old woodpecker holes. It also eats cactus fruit by the beakful and drops the seeds wherever it goes, so the cactus needs the bird just as much as the bird needs the cactus.

requirements.hint: Tall cactus to carve and split fruit to eat. A pad cactus is far too small — only a great column can hold a nest hole.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Gila Woodpecker Life History

records.name: Phainopepla
records.diet: mistletoe berries in winter, flying insects the rest of the year
records.shelter: A small cup nest in a mesquite or ironwood, usually hidden in a clump of mistletoe
records.preferredHabitat: Mesquite stands carrying mistletoe, with water nearby
records.fact: A phainopepla can put away more than a thousand mistletoe berries in a single day, and the seeds come out the other end still sticky — so the bird glues the next generation of mistletoe onto branches as it flies.
records.role: Mistletoe's one dependable gardener; almost nothing else will touch the berries. The plant only grows on mesquite, ironwood and acacia, so this glossy black bird with red eyes needs those trees as much as the mistletoe does. Out of berry season it snaps insects out of the air instead.

requirements.hint: Mistletoe in a mesquite is the whole story — the berries are dinner and the clump is the nest. It still comes down to drink.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Phainopepla Life History

records.name: Antelope Squirrel
records.diet: cactus fruit, seeds and green shoots, with the odd insect
records.shelter: Burrows and cracks under rocks and cactus
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky ground with cactus in fruit
records.fact: It runs with its tail flipped flat over its back like a tiny parasol, then throws itself belly-down on cool shaded ground to dump the heat it picked up on the way.
records.role: The one animal still out and about at midday, when everything else has gone underground to wait. It cannot make its own water, so it lives on juicy cactus fruit — which only exists if the cactus bees got to the flowers first. Coyotes, kit foxes, hawks, roadrunners and rattlesnakes all hunt it.

requirements.hint: Dry seeds alone will not keep it alive — it needs juicy fruit, and that means welcoming the bees before the squirrel.

records.name: Cactus Wren
records.diet: insects and spiders, with some cactus fruit and seeds
records.shelter: Football-shaped grass nests built deep inside a cholla
records.preferredHabitat: Desert with dense cholla and scattered trees
records.fact: A cactus wren builds several football-shaped nests and keeps the spare ones as bedrooms all year, so it goes to sleep surrounded on every side by cactus spines.
records.role: The biggest wren you will ever meet, flipping over leaves and bark for insects and spiders and taking every drop of its water from that food. Its nest sits deep inside a cholla where the spines keep snakes and raiding birds out — take away the cholla and the wren has nowhere at all to raise chicks.

requirements.hint: Cholla is the nest. Nothing else out here is spiny enough, and the wren never once needs a drink.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Cactus Wren Life History

records.name: Burrowing Owl
records.diet: big insects — termites, grasshoppers and crickets — plus small rodents and scorpions
records.shelter: Underground burrows dug by somebody else; it cannot dig its own
records.preferredHabitat: Open ground with low, sparse plants and ready-made burrows
records.fact: Corner a burrowing owl down its hole and it hisses like a rattlesnake — biologists think it is doing an impression, and whatever is digging usually decides not to.
records.role: A long-legged little owl that hunts insects in broad daylight and rodents after dark, standing on its doorstep bobbing at anything that comes near. It is the clearest case here of an animal that cannot make its own home: every pair depends on a burrow something else dug, so where the diggers go, the owls go too.

requirements.hint: It cannot dig. Bring the tortoise back first and its old den becomes the owl's front door — with low, open ground out front to hunt over.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Burrowing Owl Life History

records.name: Horned Lizard
records.diet: harvester ants above all — about nine mouthfuls in ten — plus termites and a few other insects
records.shelter: Shuffles itself down into loose sand; shelters under low shrubs
records.preferredHabitat: Open sandy ground between shrubs, near harvester ant mounds
records.fact: Cornered, a horned lizard squirts a jet of its own blood out of the corners of its eyes — it can carry a metre — and it tastes so foul that a fox will spit and keep spitting for minutes.
records.role: An ant specialist with a stomach far too big for its body, because harvester ants are such poor food that it has to eat hundreds every day just to break even. Those ants only build on open bare ground, so the tidier, greener and more trampled a desert gets, the faster this flat little lizard vanishes from it.

requirements.hint: No ants, no it. Leave the gaps between the shrubs bare and open — that is exactly where harvester ants clear their mounds.

records.name: Raven
records.diet: carrion above all, plus eggs, nestlings, young reptiles, insects and cactus fruit
records.shelter: Bulky stick nests on cliffs and in tall cactus and ironwoods — and, more and more, on power poles
records.preferredHabitat: Open desert with tall nest structures and a reliable food supply
records.fact: Ravens remember individual human faces and hold the grudge for years, and a pair will run a con together — one bird makes a nuisance of itself while the other robs the food.
records.role: The cleanup crew, and the biggest human story in the biome. Roads, rubbish tips, farms and power poles hand ravens free food, water and nest platforms, so there are now far more of them than this desert could ever feed by itself — and all those extra ravens eat baby tortoises, whose shells stay soft for years. Cutting off the free lunch is now a real part of saving the tortoise.

requirements.hint: They follow whatever gets left lying around: a carcass, a tall perch, something to drink. That is all they ask for — which is exactly the trouble.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Common Raven Life History
USFWS — Environmental Assessment to Reduce Common Raven Predation on the Desert Tortoise

records.name: Roadrunner
records.diet: lizards, big insects, millipedes, scorpions, tarantulas, small birds, rodents and snakes
records.shelter: A bulky stick nest a metre or two up inside a thorny shrub or cholla
records.preferredHabitat: Open running ground broken up by thorny thickets
records.fact: A roadrunner can outrun you — over 30 km an hour on two legs — and it kills a rattlesnake by grabbing it behind the head and beating it against a rock until it stops moving.
records.role: The daytime terror of anything small and quick: lizards, tarantulas, scorpions, millipedes, other birds, and one of the very few birds anywhere that will pick a fight with a rattlesnake. It needs both halves of its home — open ground to sprint across and a thorn thicket high enough to keep its chicks out of a coyote's reach.

requirements.hint: Open ground to run flat out on and a thorn thicket to nest in, with lizards and big crawlers to chase between the two.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Greater Roadrunner Life History

records.name: Rattlesnake
records.diet: rodents and small mammals, with birds and lizards taken now and then
records.shelter: Rock crevices and burrows; a deep frost-free fissure all winter
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky shelter within striking distance of busy rodent trails
records.fact: A rattlesnake adds a new rattle segment every time it sheds, but the old ones keep snapping off — so counting the rattles tells you nothing whatsoever about its age.
records.role: An ambush hunter that lies beside a rodent trail for days, strikes, lets go, then follows the scent trail to the body. It may eat only once a month, which makes it a slow but relentless brake on the rodent population. Every winter it goes back to the same rock den it used last year, and the year before that.

requirements.hint: A deep winter den it can come back to every single year, warm rock to wait on, and rodents on the move nearby.

sources.name: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum — Western Diamondback Rattlesnake

records.name: Scorpion
records.diet: millipedes, termites, crickets, spiders, tarantulas and other scorpions
records.shelter: A spiral burrow it digs itself, as much as two and a half metres deep
records.preferredHabitat: Loose diggable soil with litter and stone cover to hunt across at night
records.fact: Scorpions glow an eerie blue-green under ultraviolet light, and after decades of looking at it nobody can say for certain why.
records.role: The heavyweight of the night shift. Big, hairy and unhurried, it takes millipedes, termites, spiders and even tarantulas, which are its own size. The rocks are only its day cover — what actually keeps it alive is a spiral burrow driven metres straight down, where it sits out most of the year. Owls and roadrunners are the ones that get it.

requirements.hint: Rocks are only the doormat. What it really needs is soil deep and loose enough to dig metres straight down into.

records.name: Elf Owl
records.diet: moths, beetles, crickets and scorpions
records.shelter: Old woodpecker holes in cactus and desert trees; it cannot carve its own
records.preferredHabitat: Saguaro stands and mesquite washes full of old woodpecker holes
records.fact: The smallest owl in the world weighs about as much as a golf ball, and it nips the stinger off a scorpion before carrying the rest home to its chicks.
records.role: A migratory night hunter of moths and scorpions that cannot make a hole to save its life. Every nest it has ever used was chiselled out by a woodpecker and then hardened by the cactus into a waterproof boot. Plant a whole forest of cactus and you still get no elf owls until the woodpecker has done its work.

requirements.hint: Cactus alone will not do. A woodpecker has to drill the hole first and let the plant seal it into a boot.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Elf Owl Life History

records.name: Kit Fox
records.diet: kangaroo rats and other rodents, jackrabbits, squirrels, lizards, insects and some fruit
records.shelter: A cool underground den with several doors, usually a rodent burrow it has widened
records.preferredHabitat: Open desert with loose soil and plenty of small prey
records.fact: The smallest wild dog here weighs less than a house cat, and its ridiculous ears do two jobs at once: hearing a mouse move underground, and shedding body heat like radiators.
records.role: A night fox that lives almost entirely on rodents and hardly ever drinks — it takes its water out of what it catches. It rarely digs a den from scratch; it moves into a kangaroo rat's burrow and enlarges it, then keeps several doors open so a coyote can never corner it in there.

requirements.hint: Rodents first — its den is a borrowed burrow made bigger. It never needs a drink you provide.

records.name: Coyote
records.diet: voles, rabbits and ground squirrels; deer fawns; also fruit, insects and carrion
records.shelter: Raises pups in a den dug into a brushy bank, often an enlarged badger or fox burrow
records.preferredHabitat: Open grassland and edges with brushy cover for a den and water within reach
records.fact: Three coyotes can sound like a dozen. Each one slides its pitch around while it howls, so a small family throws up a wall of voices — biologists call it the 'beau geste' effect.
records.role: The animal at the top of this meadow, and the most adaptable carnivore in here. It hunts voles and rabbits alone, fawns in pairs, and eats fruit, insects and carrion in between. Its return is what finally puts pressure on the foxes, badgers and deer that nothing else here could touch — and it will happily trail a digging badger to snap up whatever bolts out the far side.

requirements.hint: A den bank tucked into brushy cover, wide grass full of rabbits and voles, and water within reach. they are the last piece — they only settle where there is already plenty to eat.

records.name: Polyphemus Moth
records.diet: as a caterpillar, tree leaves — oak, birch, hickory, maple, willow. The adult moth has no working mouth and never eats anything at all.
records.shelter: Spins a tough silk cocoon wrapped in a leaf; the cocoon falls with the leaves in autumn and overwinters on the forest floor.
records.preferredHabitat: Broadleaf woodland and woodland edge with oak, birch and hickory, and an undisturbed litter layer beneath them.
records.fact: The adult moth has no mouth. It cannot eat a single thing — everything it will ever spend finding a mate and laying eggs was eaten months earlier, by the caterpillar.
records.role: This moth stands for the caterpillar layer, the step nearly every forest bird depends on. Caterpillars turn tough, chewy tree leaves into soft protein, and it is caterpillars, not seeds, that woodland songbirds cram into their chicks. The adults that make it through feed bats at dusk. The cocoons spend all winter down in the fallen leaves, so a woodland raked bare in autumn throws next summer's moths out with the leaf bags.

requirements.hint: Broadleaf trees for the caterpillars to eat, and leaves left lying all winter for the cocoons hidden among them.

sources.name: Butterflies and Moths of North America — Antheraea polyphemus

records.name: Wood Duck
records.diet: acorns, seeds and aquatic plants; ducklings eat insects and snails for their first weeks
records.shelter: Obligate cavity nester — old woodpecker holes and natural hollows in trees over or beside water
records.preferredHabitat: Wooded ponds, sloughs and slow backwaters with big cavity trees standing in or near the water
records.fact: A wood duckling leaves home the day after it hatches by jumping out of a hole up to fifty feet up, bouncing off the ground or water, and walking away unhurt.
records.role: The wood duck is the clearest borrower in the forest: it cannot make a hole and cannot nest without one, so it turns up only after the woodpeckers do. It ferries acorns and pond-plant seeds between the woods and the water, and it feeds owls, raccoons and foxes. Wood ducks nearly vanished a century ago, and what still limits them is holes.

requirements.hint: An old woodpecker hole in a snag standing over quiet water, with oaks nearby for acorns.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Wood Duck life history

records.name: Flying Squirrel
records.diet: mostly underground truffle fungi; also lichens, acorns, tree seeds and some insects
records.shelter: Old woodpecker cavities and natural hollows; huddles in groups through winter to stay warm
records.preferredHabitat: Cool, closed-canopy hemlock and hardwood forest with old cavity trees and a deep fungal layer in the soil
records.fact: Flying squirrels do not fly, they glide — and under ultraviolet light their fur glows bubblegum pink, something nobody noticed until a researcher pointed a UV torch into the trees a few years ago.
records.role: This squirrel lives mostly on mushrooms, and mostly on underground ones it has to smell through the soil and dig up. The spores ride through it and get planted at the next set of tree roots, so squirrel, fungus and tree are one loop that keeps all three going. It cannot cut a hole either, so it sleeps in old woodpecker cavities, huddled in a heap with others for warmth — and it is the favourite meal of owls and fishers, which is how energy from the underground fungi ends up at the very top of the food web.

requirements.hint: Truffles in the soil to dig up and an old woodpecker hole to sleep in. It makes neither for itself.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service — Northern flying squirrel ecology and diet

records.name: Pileated Woodpecker
records.diet: carpenter ants and wood-boring beetle larvae above all; also berries and nuts
records.shelter: Excavates a new rectangular nest cavity each year in a large dead snag, and leaves last year's behind
records.preferredHabitat: Mature forest with large-diameter standing snags and plenty of big fallen logs on the ground
records.fact: A pileated woodpecker chisels rectangular holes so deep into rotten trunks that a small tree can snap in half where it has been working.
records.role: This is the forest's landlord. It carves a fresh nest hole every spring and never reuses the old one, and the leftovers become homes for wood ducks, flying squirrels, fishers, bats and owls — none of which can make a hole themselves. It needs two things a tidied forest lacks: standing snags fat enough to hold a cavity, and fallen logs rotted soft enough to fill with carpenter ants. Bring those back and a dozen other species follow it in.

requirements.hint: Big snags — plural, and thick — plus rotted logs on the ground crawling with carpenter ants.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Pileated Woodpecker life history

records.name: Skunk
records.diet: beetle grubs and insects dug out of the soil, plus eggs, berries and mice
records.shelter: A borrowed burrow or a hollow under a log, plugged with leaves in the coldest weeks
records.preferredHabitat: Forest edges and clearings with soft diggable ground and plenty of cover
records.fact: A skunk would much rather not spray you. First it stamps its front feet, then it hisses, then it does a handstand — and only if you ignore all three does it turn around and fire, accurately, from about three metres.
records.role: The forest's night gardener. It spends the dark hours digging little cone-shaped holes across the floor hunting beetle grubs, turning over the soil as it goes, and almost nothing dares hunt it — except the great horned owl, which has no sense of smell worth mentioning.

requirements.hint: Soft, diggable earth full of grubs, and a hollow log to sleep the day away in. they want somewhere to dig more than somewhere to hide.

records.name: Fisher
records.diet: small and medium mammals — porcupines, squirrels, hares — plus birds, carrion and fruit
records.shelter: Dens in hollow logs and ground burrows; kits are raised in a cavity high inside a living tree
records.preferredHabitat: Unbroken conifer and mixed forest with a closed canopy and large hollow trees
records.fact: The fisher is one of the only animals that eats porcupines. It circles round to the face — the one place with no quills — and keeps biting until it can flip the porcupine over and reach the belly.
records.role: The fisher treats the treetops like the ground, chasing squirrels through branches and catching flying squirrels most predators never even see, and it is the main check on porcupine numbers. Because it needs canopy that connects tree to tree and big trees hollow enough to raise kits inside, finding a fisher tells you the forest is old and joined up rather than cut into patches.

requirements.hint: Closed canopy overhead, a big living tree hollow enough to raise kits high off the ground, and they below to hunt.

records.name: American Goldfinch
records.diet: almost entirely seeds — thistle, sunflower, aster and grass seed
records.shelter: A tight cup nest lashed a few feet up in a shrub, bound with spider silk and lined with thistle down
records.preferredHabitat: Weedy fields and open ground with native thistle, sunflower and asters left standing
records.fact: Goldfinches are such strict vegetarians that a cowbird chick sneaked into a goldfinch nest starves — it cannot survive on an all-seed diet.
records.role: A seed specialist that waits until midsummer to nest, when thistle down is finally ready to line the cup. It feeds its chicks on seed rather than insects, which almost no other songbird does, and it scatters thistle and sunflower seed across the meadow as it feeds. Being small and everywhere makes it a favourite of bird-catching hawks.

requirements.hint: Let the sunflowers and native thistles stand and go to seed. The down is what the late nest is lined with, so don't cut them back in autumn.

sources.name: Cornell All About Birds — American Goldfinch
Xerces Society — Standing Up for Native Thistles

records.name: Praying Mantis
records.diet: live insects seized by ambush — grasshoppers, bees, butterflies and anything else that walks past
records.shelter: Perches motionless on plants; glues a foam egg case to a stiff standing stem for the winter
records.preferredHabitat: Meadows and flowery edges with standing vegetation to ambush from
records.fact: A mantis has one ear, in the middle of its chest, and it is tuned to bat calls. When it hears a bat hunting it folds its wings and power-dives out of the sky.
records.role: A sit-still ambush hunter that snaps out its spined forelegs faster than you can blink and swivels its head almost right around to watch you. It is not a pest-control specialist — it takes whatever comes past, which means grasshoppers, but also bumble bees, leafcutter bees and monarch caterpillars. Bluebirds, meadowlarks, garter snakes and bats take it in turn.

requirements.hint: Leave stiff dead stems standing through the winter. That's where the foam egg case is glued, and cutting them back in autumn cuts next summer's mantises.

sources.name: NC State Extension — Challenging the conventional wisdom about praying mantids

records.name: Bluebird
records.diet: ground insects — caterpillars, beetles, grasshoppers — plus berries in winter
records.shelter: Grass-lined nest inside a tree cavity, an old woodpecker hole or a nest box
records.preferredHabitat: Grassy openings with scattered trees and low perches to drop from
records.fact: A bluebird can spot a caterpillar on the ground from the top of a fencepost twenty metres away, drop on it, and be back on the post before you've noticed it left.
records.role: Bluebirds hunt by perching, staring at short grass, and dropping. They cannot cut their own nest hole, so they take over holes something else made — and in a meadow with no woodpecker, that means a nest box. Volunteers putting up box trails are a large part of why this bird came back at all.

requirements.hint: It can't make its own hole. Put a box up facing open grass, keep the grass short enough to hunt over, and add berries for the winter.

sources.name: Cornell All About Birds — Eastern Bluebird

records.name: American Badger
records.diet: ground squirrels, gophers, voles and mice dug straight out of their tunnels; also insects and bumble bee nests
records.shelter: Digs its own large burrows; one of the fastest excavators alive
records.preferredHabitat: Open grassland with deep, stone-free, diggable soil and a rodent colony to work
records.fact: A badger can dig itself completely out of sight in under a minute — and it sometimes hunts alongside a coyote, the badger going in from below while the coyote grabs whatever bolts out of the top.
records.role: A carnivore that hunts by excavation, going down a squirrel or gopher tunnel after its owner. That only works in deep stone-free soil, and only where there is a rodent colony worth the digging. The big holes it leaves behind get reused by foxes, coyotes and burrowing insects for years afterwards. Adults are safe from almost everything; cubs are not.

requirements.hint: Deep stone-free soil it can tear through, wide grass on top, and a ground squirrel colony to hunt. Rock piles are the opposite of what it wants.

records.name: Freshwater Shrimp
records.diet: dead leaves and stems, the fungi and bacteria growing on them, and algal film scraped off plants.
records.shelter: Among submerged litter, plant stems and the loose top layer of sediment.
records.preferredHabitat: Shallow, well-oxygenated water with a deep drift of decaying plant litter.
records.fact: Freshwater shrimp swim on their sides, and males carry females around piggyback for days before they mate. Lift a handful of soggy leaves out of a pond and dozens of them will be flicking about in it.
records.role: The marsh's shredder. One shrimp chews a single dead cattail leaf into thousands of crumbs — and it is really after the fungus furring the leaf, not the leaf itself. That is how a heap of dead plants becomes food for minnows, salamander larvae and dragonfly nymphs.

requirements.hint: A drift of rotting leaves in still water is all they need.

sources.name: Biological Invasions — Potential impact of invasive amphipods on leaf litter recycling in aquatic ecosystems

records.name: Crayfish
records.diet: decaying plants and carcasses, live aquatic plants, snails, insect larvae and freshwater shrimp.
records.shelter: Burrows dug into saturated banks, and gaps beneath sunken logs and stones.
records.preferredHabitat: Slow, weedy water with woody cover and a bank soft enough to dig into.
records.fact: Lose a claw in a fight and a crayfish just grows a new one, a little bigger at every moult, until it matches the old one. Startle it and it flips its tail and rockets backwards faster than you can grab.
records.role: The marsh's recycler, and very nearly everybody's dinner. Crayfish shred dead plants and tidy up carcasses, turning buried gunk back into living meat — which the otter, the mink, the kingfisher, the merganser, the crane, the snapping turtle and the heron then come and take.

requirements.hint: A soft bank to tunnel into, sunken wood to hide under, and plenty of rotting plants to eat.

sources.name: Reviews in Fisheries Science — Redefining the role of crayfish in aquatic ecosystems
Oecologia — Effects of crayfish on leaf processing and invertebrate colonisation of leaves

records.name: Freshwater Mussel
records.diet: algae, bacteria and fine dead particles strained out of the water.
records.shelter: Burrowed upright in stable fine sediment with only its two siphons showing.
records.preferredHabitat: Slow, settled water over firm silt and fine sand.
records.fact: A baby mussel has to hitchhike. It clamps onto the gills of a passing fish and rides there for weeks before dropping off to start life on the bottom — and some mother mussels wave a flap of flesh shaped like a little fish to lure a host in close.
records.role: The marsh's water filter, and one of the longest-lived animals in it. One mussel can strain the same patch of water for thirty years, dropping what it catches to the bottom for shrimp and crayfish. No fish means no baby mussels, so the mussels only come back after the minnows do.

requirements.hint: A settled bed that stays put for years — and fish, because young they ride to their new home clamped to fish gills.

sources.name: NC Wildlife — General Life History for Mussels

records.name: Leopard Frog
records.diet: insects, spiders and worms taken in wet meadows and along the water's edge
records.shelter: Shallow water in spring; damp grassy meadow through the summer
records.preferredHabitat: Lily-fringed shallows with wet meadow beside them
records.fact: A startled leopard frog leaps in zig-zags away from the water instead of towards it — and the second it lands in long grass those big dark spots break its outline up and it vanishes.
records.role: The frog that leaves the pond. It spends the whole summer hunting insects out in damp meadow and only hops back to the water in autumn, which is why a marsh mown right to the waterline loses its leopard frogs first.

requirements.hint: A lily pool to breed in and a wide band of damp meadow beside it to spend the whole summer hunting in.

sources.name: National Park Service — Northern Leopard Frog

records.name: Marsh Wren
records.diet: insects and spiders picked from marsh stems
records.shelter: Woven dome nests lashed among cattails and bulrushes
records.preferredHabitat: Cattail and bulrush stands over water
records.fact: A male marsh wren builds up to a dozen empty practice nests for one female to come and inspect — and while he is at it he will sneak into a neighbour's nest and punch holes in the eggs.
records.role: A thumb-sized bird with an enormous attitude. It runs up and down reed stems picking off spiders and insects, stitches hanging ball nests between the stiff stalks, and robs the eggs of anything that nests too close.

requirements.hint: Bulrush and cattail standing in water — stiff stems a wren can weave a hanging ball nest between.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Marsh Wren life history

records.name: Snapping Turtle
records.diet: carrion, fish, crayfish, aquatic plants and almost anything else it can catch
records.shelter: Muddy pond bottoms; females travel overland to sandy banks to nest
records.preferredHabitat: Deep still water with a soft mud bottom and a sandy rise to nest on
records.fact: A snapping turtle is too big to pull into its own shell, so it does not bother trying. Underwater it is calm and shy and will swim away from you — the famous snap only comes out when it is stranded on dry land with nowhere left to hide.
records.role: The marsh's bulldozer and its clean-up crew, walking the bottom eating carrion, plants, fish and the occasional duckling. Grown adults are almost untouchable; it is the eggs everything digs up, which is why one good nest bank matters more than any single old turtle.

requirements.hint: Deep still water with a soft bottom, plus a warm sandy rise above the waterline for the females to dig their nests in.

records.name: Kingfisher
records.diet: small fish and crayfish
records.shelter: Tunnel burrows dug a metre or more into bare earthen banks
records.preferredHabitat: Clear water with a bare vertical bank beside it and perches overhead
records.fact: A kingfisher shuts its eyes just before it hits the water, so the last part of the dive is flown blind from memory. Then it whacks the fish against a branch and swallows it head-first so the fins fold the right way.
records.role: The rattling plunge-diver of the marsh, and one of the rare birds where the female is the flashier of the pair. It digs its own nest tunnel a metre back into a bare earth bank, so a marsh stuffed with fish but with no raw bank still gets no kingfishers.

requirements.hint: Clear open water to dive into and a bare vertical earth bank to tunnel into. A nest box is no use to a bird that digs its own.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Belted Kingfisher life history

records.name: Merganser
records.diet: small fish, crayfish, dragonfly nymphs and other aquatic insects
records.shelter: Tree cavities in standing dead timber over or beside water
records.preferredHabitat: Quiet ponds with drowned standing trees
records.fact: Merganser ducklings jump out of a tree hole up to fifteen metres above the ground the day after they hatch, bounce off the leaf litter unhurt, and are diving for their own food within a day of landing.
records.role: A tiny diving duck with a fold-out white fan on its head, a saw-edged bill for gripping slippery fish, and a clear third eyelid it wears like swimming goggles. It nests in holes in drowned trees, which makes a beaver pond exactly its sort of place.

requirements.hint: A wooded pond with dead trees still standing in it. The hen wants a hole in a drowned alder — a nest box is only a stand-in.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Hooded Merganser life history

records.name: Pillbug
records.diet: dead leaves, rotting wood, grass thatch and fungal threads; also droppings and old bones for minerals
records.shelter: Hides by day under crumbling logs, flat stones and deep litter, where the air stays damp
records.preferredHabitat: Shaded, damp corners of meadow with rotting wood and a thick layer of dead plant litter
records.fact: A pillbug is not an insect at all — it's a crustacean, closer kin to a crab than to a beetle, and it still breathes through gill-like flaps that have to stay wet.
records.role: Pillbugs work the night shift under logs and thatch, shredding dead leaves and soft rotten wood into crumbs small enough for fungi and bacteria to finish off. That shredding is the first step in turning last year's meadow into next year's soil. Garter snakes and killdeer hunt them, so the recycling crew feeds upward as well as downward.

requirements.hint: Damp, dark and rotting is the whole recipe — a crumbling log, deep thatch, and ground that never dries right out. Roll one over and it curls into a ball.

records.name: Garden Spider
records.diet: flying and jumping insects caught in the web — grasshoppers, bees, flies, moths
records.shelter: Hangs head-down at the hub of its own orb web, slung between tall standing stems
records.preferredHabitat: Sunny meadow with tall stiff vegetation left standing and plenty of flying insects
records.fact: This spider takes down most of its web every night and eats the old silk to build the next one — and it stitches a bold white zigzag through the middle that nobody has fully explained yet.
records.role: The meadow's trapper. It slings a wheel of silk wider than your hand between tall stems and waits head-down at the hub for grasshoppers, bees and flies to blunder in.
