Spiders are the largest predator group in any grassland and the biggest single thing missing from this meadow until now — they eat enormous numbers of insects, and they are in turn the main food of half the songbirds here.

requirements.hint: Tall stiff stems left standing, spaced far enough apart to sling a big web between them, with flowers close by to bring the insects in.

sources.name: UF/IFAS Featured Creatures — yellow garden spider

records.name: Brown Bat
records.diet: night-flying insects, especially beetles, plus moths, flying ants and midges
records.shelter: Roosts by day in warm dark spaces — barn lofts, attics, and under loose bark; hibernates in cold cracks
records.preferredHabitat: Open meadow and hedgerow airspace to hunt over, with still water to drink from and a warm roost nearby
records.fact: A big brown bat finds a moth in total darkness by shouting and listening to the echo — and it can pick out something no thicker than a pencil lead this way.
records.role: The night shift over the meadow. Big brown bats work the air above the grass and along the hedgerows after sunset, catching beetles, moths and flying ants; one bat can put away thousands of insects in a single night. They drink on the wing, dipping their jaws into still water without stopping, and mothers gather in warm roosts to raise pups together. Great horned owls catch them at dusk.

requirements.hint: A warm crevice to raise pups in, insects in the air above the grass, and calm open water it can skim a drink from without landing.

sources.name: Bat Conservation International — Big Brown Bat

records.name: Barn Owl
records.diet: almost entirely small mammals under about 100 grams — voles, mice and shrews
records.shelter: Nests and roosts in a dark high cavity: a barn loft, a hollow tree, or a large nest box. Builds nothing itself
records.preferredHabitat: Wide open grassland to hunt over, with a dark cavity above ground to sleep and nest in
records.fact: A barn owl can catch a mouse in complete darkness by sound alone. One ear sits higher than the other, so it hears in three dimensions — and the fringed edges of its wings mean the mouse never hears it coming.
records.role: The meadow works a night shift, and the barn owl runs it. While the hawk and the coyote hunt by daylight, this one quarters the same grass in the dark on silent wings, living almost entirely on voles — a single family can take well over a thousand of them in a year. Nothing here hunts the barn owl back.

requirements.hint: A dark loft or a deep box up off the ground, wide grass to quarter over, and a meadow already full of voles. Owls take their water from their prey.

sources.name: Cornell All About Birds — American Barn Owl
American Ornithological Society — 65th Supplement to the Check-list

records.name: Mountain Lion
records.diet: deer and wild sheep mostly, plus jackrabbits, foxes and anything else it can get close enough to
records.shelter: No fixed home; the kittens are hidden in a dry cave or overhang in a canyon wall
records.preferredHabitat: Broken canyon country with ledges, boulders and brush to stalk through, and somewhere reliable to drink
records.fact: The biggest cat out here cannot roar. It purrs like a house cat, screams like something out of a nightmare, and can jump five metres straight up onto a ledge from standing.
records.role: The top of the desert food chain and a pure ambush hunter — it does not chase things down, it gets close and then explodes. Because it kills by stalking, it needs broken ground and brush to hide in; out on the open flat it goes hungry. It drags a big kill into cover and buries it under sticks and sand to come back to for days, which quietly feeds ravens, foxes and half the beetles in the wash. Kittens spend their first weeks tucked into a cave in a canyon wall, and nothing out here hunts a grown lion.

requirements.hint: Big prey first, then rough broken ground to stalk through and a sheltered overhang for the kittens. Unlike most things out here it does come down to drink. It is the last animal to come back.

records.name: Snail
records.diet: dead leaves, soft rotting stems, and the algae film on damp stones
records.shelter: Seals itself to the underside of a damp log or stone and waits out dry weather
records.preferredHabitat: Shady, damp corners with leaf litter and something chalky to rasp at
records.fact: A snail carries its own house and can shut the door behind it — when things get dry it glues itself to a stone and sleeps until it rains, sometimes for months.
records.role: Snails are the meadow's slow recyclers. They shred fallen leaves into crumbs that fungi and soil life can finish off, and their shells give calcium back to the ground when they die.

requirements.hint: A shady damp corner where leaves are allowed to pile up and rot. they want the mess, not the tidy bit.

records.name: Mountain Goat
records.diet: grasses, sedges and alpine forbs in summer; lichen, moss and shrub twigs scraped off rock in winter
records.shelter: Beds scraped out on narrow cliff ledges and in shallow caves under overhangs
records.preferredHabitat: The steepest broken cliff and ledge ground above the treeline, with turf to graze and a mineral seep within reach
records.fact: A mountain goat's hooves split apart as it steps, gripping stone like the rubber on climbing shoes, and it will sleep on a ledge no wider than a doormat with a 300-metre drop underneath it.
records.role: The white climber of the high cliffs, grazing turf and lichen and then retreating onto ground so steep that almost nothing can follow. That is the whole trick: goats live where other big grazers simply cannot go. They will walk for hours to a mineral lick and shove each other around at it. Mountain lions are the real threat, while eagles and wolverines take kids. In some ranges goats are native and in others people brought them in, so a white goat on a skyline is not always a local.

requirements.hint: Steeper is better. Give it cliff ledges to bed on, turf to graze between them, and a mineral lick, because goats will travel for hours to eat salty ground. Do not expect one out on the open flats.

records.name: Wolverine
records.diet: marmots, hares and ptarmigan when it can catch them, frozen carcasses when it cannot, and berries in late summer
records.shelter: Tunnels dug metres down into deep spring drifts, usually around a fallen boulder or log, with food stored in side chambers
records.preferredHabitat: Big, empty, high country with talus and broken rock, and snow that lasts into late spring
records.fact: A wolverine can smell a dead animal buried under three metres of snow, dig it out, and then drive a bear off it, all in a body about the size of a small dog.
records.role: The largest weasel in the world and the mountain's great scavenger, now the top hunter on these peaks. It roams enormous distances, kills marmots, hares and ptarmigan when it gets the chance and lives off frozen carcasses when it does not, cracking frozen bone with jaws built for exactly that. Snow is its refrigerator: it stores food in drifts and dens deep inside them, so a female can only raise kits where the snowpack holds into late spring. That makes it the first animal to go when winters get short — and nothing up here is willing to argue with it over a carcass.

requirements.hint: They need space and snow, not scenery. Give it drifts deep enough to last into late spring for the den and the larder, broken rock to travel through, and marmots and hares already on the mountain. It is the last of the hunters to arrive.

records.name: Sea Turtle
records.diet: seagrass above all — eelgrass and surfgrass — plus sea lettuce and other soft algae
records.shelter: Sleeps wedged under ledges or resting on quiet sand and gravel bottom between grazing trips
records.preferredHabitat: Warm summer water in a sheltered bay with seagrass meadows to graze
records.fact: Adult green sea turtles are the only sea turtles that eat plants, and their jaws are serrated like bread knives for sawing through seagrass. They crop the same patch again and again, which keeps it short and tender — a turtle basically mows a lawn on the seafloor.
records.role: A summer visitor that swims in from warmer water to eat, not to nest — no turtle lays eggs on a cool coast like this one. Grazing adults keep the seagrass cropped and growing fresh instead of going long and shaggy, and they are the only animal here besides the brant that eats a seagrass meadow for a living.

requirements.hint: This one comes for the grazing, not the sand, so do not build it a nest beach. Warm summer water, a cropped grazing lawn out in the eelgrass, and quiet bottom to sleep on between meals.

records.name: Bottlenose Dolphin
records.diet: schooling fish, especially anchovy, plus squid and bottom fish
records.shelter: None built — travels and sleeps at sea in a small group, half its brain awake at a time
records.preferredHabitat: Nearshore water along an open beach with a strong surf line and fish schools offshore
records.fact: Every dolphin invents its own signature whistle, and the others copy that whistle back when they want to call it over. Along an open beach these dolphins hunt right inside the breakers, surfing the waves they are herding fish against.
records.role: Fast, social hunters that work the surf line in small groups, pushing anchovy schools up against the breaking waves until the fish have nowhere left to go. They are quick and clever enough to catch almost anything that schools here — and still not the biggest thing in the water.

requirements.hint: Deep water to travel through, cold currents and kelp edges to hold the fish, and a real breaking surf line, because that is where these dolphins do their hunting.

sources.name: Janik & King 2013, Proc R Soc B — Vocal copying of individually distinctive signature whistles

records.name: Orca
records.diet: marine mammals — harbor seals above all, plus dolphins, sea lions and gray whale calves
records.shelter: None ashore; rests at the surface in deep water with its family pod
records.preferredHabitat: Cold deep water close inshore, along the drop-off and the kelp edge within reach of seal haul-outs
records.fact: Orcas live in families that never split up, and different families eat completely different food. The ones that hunt this coast are mammal specialists, and they go silent to do it — no clicks, no calls — because a seal can hear a talking orca coming from a long way off.
records.role: The top of this coast, with nothing above it. A pod of mammal-hunting orcas patrols the drop-off where the seafloor falls away, listening at seal haul-outs and shadowing gray whales that pass through with calves in spring. When they come into a bay, every seal on the rocks goes still and silent.

requirements.hint: The last and hardest animal to bring back. they need deep water pressed right up against the shore and something big to hunt — so bring the seals back first, because the seals are what they come for.

records.name: Desert Millipede
records.diet: dead leaves, stems, seed husks and other dry plant litter on the ground
records.shelter: Buried in soil and tucked under litter and rock slabs by day; out walking on damp nights
records.preferredHabitat: Litter drifts under shrubs with rock slabs and diggable soil nearby
records.fact: A desert millipede spends most of the year underground, then comes pouring out by the hundreds after the first summer storm — and if you touch one it coils into a tight spiral like a cinnamon bun and oozes a bitter brown liquid that stains your fingers for days.
records.role: The litter shredder. It chews dead leaves, stems and husks into crumbs small enough for termites and soil microbes to finish, which is how dead plants become soil again out here. It has hundreds of legs and absolutely no hurry — armour and a foul chemical mean it can afford to stroll — but scorpions and roadrunners eat it anyway.

requirements.hint: Let the leaves drift up under the shrubs and leave a slab it can crawl beneath. Damp litter is both its dinner and its hiding place — bare hot sand is neither.

sources.name: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum — Millipedes and Centipedes

records.name: Desert Tarantula
records.diet: crickets, beetles, grasshoppers, termites and other spiders
records.shelter: A silk-lined burrow in firm soil, its doorway strung with trip-lines
records.preferredHabitat: Firm open ground between shrubs with litter and cover close by
records.fact: A frightened tarantula rubs its back legs over its belly and flicks off a cloud of barbed hairs that itch like fibreglass — and if nothing comes past to eat, it can simply wait, going a whole year between meals.
records.role: A patient ambush hunter that lives at the mouth of a silk-lined burrow, feeling for the twitch of a cricket on the trip-lines at its door. A female may keep the same hole for twenty years, which makes her one of the longest-lived animals in the biome. Roadrunners take them — and so does the giant hairy scorpion, which outweighs a tarantula and is not remotely afraid of one.

requirements.hint: Firm ground it can line with silk, and then quiet. A burrow a tarantula digs is a burrow she may still be sitting in twenty years from now.

records.name: Desert Hawk
records.diet: jackrabbits, ground squirrels, quail, woodrats and lizards
records.shelter: A bulky stick nest wedged in the arms of a tall cactus or a thorny tree, built and guarded by the whole family
records.preferredHabitat: Open scrub with tall cactus and trees to nest and keep lookout from
records.fact: These are the only birds of prey in the world that hunt in packs: a family of five or six spreads out, some crashing into a thorn bush to panic a rabbit while the others wait on the far side. And when there is nowhere decent to perch, they simply stand on each other's backs, three hawks high.
records.role: The daytime top predator, working the same desert the coyote works at night. Two or three generations live together all year, share every kill, help feed each other's chicks and take turns on lookout — teamwork that lets them bring down jackrabbits far heavier than any single hawk. They need tall lookouts above open ground and a big cactus solid enough to hold a family nest.

requirements.hint: One hawk is never the whole story. A family needs a tall cactus strong enough to hold the nest, high lookouts all around it, and open ground with rabbits crossing it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Harris's Hawk Life History

records.name: Elk
records.diet: grass and leafy plants through the growing season; twigs, buds, bark and acorns once the green is gone
records.shelter: No den — beds down in thick conifer cover by day and moves out into open gaps to feed at dawn and dusk
records.preferredHabitat: Big blocks of forest broken by clearings and young regrowth to graze, thick cover to rest in, and a muddy wallow within a day's walk
records.fact: A bull elk grows a whole new set of antlers every year, laying down up to an inch of bone a day — the fastest-growing bone of any animal — and drops the lot each spring. In autumn he bugles: a squeal that carries more than a mile from an animal the size of a horse.
records.role: The elk is this forest's big grazer, and the only animal here that eats grass in bulk. Where a squirrel nibbles and a porcupine peels bark, a herd of elk crops whole clearings, keeping gaps open and sunlit so the plants and insects of the forest edge have somewhere to live — and grazing them bare if there are too many. Elk churn wallows into muddy pools that frogs and insects then breed in, carry seeds in their coats and droppings, and their calves are one of the few big meals a bear can find in spring. Elk vanished from these woods for more than a century and are back only where people put them back.

requirements.hint: Grassy gaps and young regrowth to graze, thick cover to rest in, and a muddy wallow to roll in — a bull plasters himself in mud before he starts bugling.

records.name: Towhee
records.diet: insects, spiders and millipedes kicked out of the leaf litter, plus seeds, berries and bits of acorn
records.shelter: Nests on the ground in dead leaves beneath a bramble or dense shrub, the cup sunk level with the surface
records.preferredHabitat: Brushy tangles, forest edges and sunlit gaps where young growth is thick and the ground is deep in fallen leaves
records.fact: That loud rustling in the dead leaves usually isn't a deer — it's a bird the size of your hand, kicking backwards with both feet at once to flip the leaves over and see what's underneath.
records.role: The towhee works a layer nothing else in this forest bothers with: the top couple of inches of dead leaves. Its two-footed backwards kick turns litter over and over while it hunts the insects, spiders and millipedes hiding there, and the seeds and berries it swallows come back out along the brushy edges. Because the nest sits flat on the ground, the towhee feeds foxes and snakes — and it can only nest where the brush overhead is thick enough to hide a cup of grass.

requirements.hint: Thick young brush standing over a deep, unraked leaf layer. The nest goes on the ground, so the tangle above it has to be dense enough to hide it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Eastern Towhee life history

records.name: Water Strider
records.diet: insects and spiders trapped in the surface film, plus mosquito larvae hanging just underneath it.
records.shelter: Sheltered, wind-free water; overwinters tucked under bank litter and floating debris.
records.preferredHabitat: Smooth, calm pockets of open water out of the wind, with floating stems to rest and lay eggs on.
records.fact: Water striders do not swim — they stand on the water. Thousands of tiny hairs on each foot trap air and refuse to get wet, and the strider reads ripples the way a spider reads its web to find insects thrashing on the surface.
records.role: The marsh's surface patrol, and one of the first animals back once the water is clean and still. Striders skate over the film eating whatever falls in and cannot climb out, and they are themselves easy pickings for minnows, frogs, dragonflies and blackbirds.

requirements.hint: Striders need calm. Find a pocket of water the wind cannot ruffle, with floating stems on it to rest and lay eggs on.

sources.name: Nature — The hydrodynamics of water strider locomotion

records.name: Bald Eagle
records.diet: mostly fish, plus ducks, muskrats and carrion — and anything it can bully out of another hunter's grip
records.shelter: A huge stick nest in the crown of the tallest living tree beside open water, added to every year
records.preferredHabitat: Wide open water full of fish, with one very tall tree to watch it all from
records.fact: A bald eagle would honestly rather rob than fish. It shadows otters and herons and harasses them until they drop their catch, then takes it — and the nest it rebuilds every year can end up heavier than a small car.
records.role: The top predator of the marsh and its biggest bully. It takes fish, ducks and muskrats for itself, kills herons at their nesting colonies, and spends much of the day stealing meals from otters and herons — which means it can only settle somewhere those hunters are already doing well.
eatsOther: fish stolen from otters and herons

requirements.hint: One huge old tree with a clear view over deep water, enough fish to live on — and successful otters and herons below to steal from.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Bald Eagle life history

records.name: Luna Moth
records.diet: hickory, walnut, sweetgum and birch leaves as a caterpillar; the adult eats nothing at all
records.shelter: A papery cocoon spun inside a curled leaf that falls to the ground, where it lies buried in the litter all winter
records.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous woodland with deep undisturbed leaf litter under the host trees
records.fact: An adult luna moth has no mouth. It hatches out with about a week to live, never eats once, and spends the whole of it looking for a mate.
records.role: Luna moth caterpillars are leaf-eaters that turn tree leaves into fat, high-energy insect bodies, and everything from bats to jays cashes that in. The long twisted tails on the hindwings are an anti-bat device: they spin as the moth flies and throw a bat's echolocation off target, so the bat grabs a tail streamer instead of the body. Because the cocoon overwinters in fallen leaves, a forest that gets raked loses its luna moths even if every host tree is still standing.

requirements.hint: Plant the leafy trees, then let the leaves lie where they fall. The cocoons spend the whole winter down in that litter.

sources.name: Butterflies and Moths of North America — Actias luna

records.name: Blue Jay
records.diet: acorns and beechnuts, caterpillars, beetles and other insects, and eggs or nestlings when it finds them
records.shelter: A cup of twigs and rootlets wedged in a fork high in a leafy tree, screened by foliage
records.preferredHabitat: Oak-rich woodland and its edges, with open ground nearby for caching
records.fact: Blue jay feathers are not actually blue — the pigment in them is brown, and the blue is a trick of light bouncing off tiny air pockets. Crush one and the colour disappears.
records.role: A single blue jay can carry five acorns at a time and bury a few thousand in an autumn, and it chooses sound ones and pushes them into open ground — which makes jays the fastest tree planters in the forest and the reason oaks spread uphill after a fire. Jays also mimic hawk calls, sometimes to clear a feeding spot and sometimes to warn everything nearby that a real hawk has arrived, so the whole wood listens to them.

requirements.hint: Oaks and a patch of soft open ground to bury the acorns in. Some of the ones the jay forgets will be your next oak trees.

records.name: Wood Frog
records.diet: beetles, spiders, slugs, flies and other small forest-floor invertebrates
records.shelter: Shallow leaf litter and loose duff on the forest floor — it does not burrow below the frost line
records.preferredHabitat: Damp deciduous forest with fishless woodland pools that fill in spring and dry out by late summer
records.fact: A wood frog freezes solid every winter. Its heart stops, two thirds of the water in its body turns to ice, and in spring it thaws out and hops away.
records.role: Wood frogs are the first amphibian to call in spring, breeding in temporary pools that dry up before fish can ever live in them — which is exactly why the tadpoles survive. Sugar flooding the blood keeps their cells from bursting while they are frozen, so they can hibernate under a few centimetres of leaves. As adults they eat their way through the invertebrates of the leaf litter and are eaten in turn by snakes and raccoons, moving forest-floor energy up the food chain.

requirements.hint: A pool that dries up in summer is the good kind — no fish means the tadpoles live. Keep deep leaves nearby for the frogs to freeze in.

records.name: Goshawk
records.diet: squirrels, jays, grouse, rabbits and woodpeckers, chased down inside the trees
records.shelter: A broad stick nest built against the trunk on a heavy limb, halfway up a big old tree in closed canopy
records.preferredHabitat: Mature forest with a high closed canopy and open flying room underneath it
records.fact: A goshawk hunts by crashing straight through the branches at full speed with its wings half folded, and it will dive at anything — including people — that walks too near its nest.
records.role: The goshawk is the forest's top daytime hunter and the reason squirrels freeze against tree trunks. Short broad wings and a long steering tail let it turn inside a wood at speed, so unlike a soaring hawk it hunts under the canopy rather than above it. It needs old forest with big limbs to nest on and clear space beneath to fly, which makes its arrival a sign that the trees have finally grown up.

requirements.hint: Grow the forest tall and leave the understory open. It needs a big limb to nest on and room to fly hard between the trunks.

records.name: Moose
records.diet: submerged pondweed and water lilies in summer, willow and aspen twigs in winter
records.shelter: Beds pressed into willow thickets and shaded marsh edge; in summer it stands chest-deep in water to escape flies
records.preferredHabitat: Marsh and pond edge with deep willow thickets and clear shallow water full of submerged plants
records.fact: A moose can hold its breath for a minute and walk along the bottom of a pond with its whole head underwater, pulling up plants by the roots.
records.role: Moose come to the wetland for sodium, which the submerged plants have and the forest browse does not, and a big one can pull 20 kilograms of pondweed a day out of the shallows. That heavy grazing keeps open lanes through the plant beds where ducks feed and fish shelter, and the willow they browse in winter grows back thicker and lower — which is better cover for everything small. Their trails through the marsh become channels that hold water in dry summers.

requirements.hint: Grow the underwater plant beds first and keep the water clear. It comes for what is growing under the surface, not on the bank.

sources.name: National Park Service, Isle Royale — Moose

records.name: River Cooter
records.diet: pondweed, algae, water lily leaves and fallen fruit; hatchlings take insects before switching to plants
records.shelter: Sleeps wedged under submerged logs and root tangles; spends the winter buried in the mud of the pond bottom
records.preferredHabitat: Slow, plant-filled water with logs to bask on and an open sunlit bank to lay eggs in
records.fact: Whether a cooter's eggs hatch into males or females depends on how warm the nest is, not on the eggs themselves — a cool nest makes brothers, a warm one makes sisters.
records.role: The cooter is the wetland's big plant-eating turtle, cropping the underwater meadows and keeping them from choking the shallows, and passing seeds out intact somewhere else. It has to bask for hours to get warm enough to digest all that plant food, which is why a good log stacked with turtles is a sign of a working marsh. Its eggs and hatchlings feed almost everything else, so it lays a lot of them.

requirements.hint: Logs in the sun to bask on and a bare warm bank to bury eggs in. A cooter that cannot get warm cannot digest its dinner.

records.name: Javelina
records.diet: prickly pear pads, mesquite pods, agave hearts, roots and tubers
records.shelter: Beds down as a herd in the shade of dense thornscrub or a rock overhang through the heat of the day
records.preferredHabitat: Desert scrub and washes with thick thorny cover and stands of prickly pear
records.fact: A javelina eats prickly pear whole — spines and all — and has a scent gland on its back so strong that a herd can find each other in the dark by smell alone.
records.role: Javelinas are the desert's cactus processors: they crunch through pads that nothing else will touch, which keeps prickly pear from taking over a wash and spreads its seeds in their droppings. Rooting for tubers turns over hard-crusted soil and buries litter, giving seeds somewhere to germinate after rain. They travel in herds of six to a dozen, and the herd smell is also the alarm system, because their eyesight is terrible.

requirements.hint: Grow the prickly pear and leave a shaded thorny tangle to bed down in. A herd sleeps out the middle of the day and feeds at dusk.

records.name: Black Swift
records.diet: flying ants, aphids, beetles and mayflies caught on the wing, often hundreds of metres up
records.shelter: A cup of moss glued to a wet rock seam behind or beside falling water, reached only from the air
records.preferredHabitat: Cliffs with cold running water and wide open sky above the treeline
records.fact: A black swift can stay in the air for six months without landing once — it eats, drinks and sleeps flying, and the chick is left alone all day while its parents hunt insects 50 km away.
records.role: Swifts hoover up the swarming insects that get lifted onto the mountain by rising air, and they carry that food back as a compressed pellet — one delivery a day is enough for a chick because the load is so concentrated. The nest has to be permanently wet and unreachable, so the birds only appear where there is a cliff seam with water running over it. They are among the very last summer visitors to arrive and the first to leave for the Amazon.
eatsOther: aphids carried up on the wind

requirements.hint: Find the wettest, darkest crack in the cliff and keep the water running down it. A swift will not nest anywhere it can walk to.

records.name: Peregrine Falcon
records.diet: other birds taken in mid-air — ptarmigan, rosy-finches, swifts, pipits and small ducks
records.shelter: A bare scrape kicked into gravel on a high cliff ledge; it builds no nest at all
records.preferredHabitat: Sheer cliffs and rock faces overlooking open ground with plenty of birds flying below
records.fact: A stooping peregrine hits about 380 km/h, which makes it the fastest animal alive — and it has bony cones in its nostrils that slow the air down so the dive does not burst its lungs.
records.role: The peregrine is the mountain's aerial hunter, and it takes almost all of its food in the air, striking from above with a closed fist rather than grabbing. Because it hunts birds and nothing else, it is a direct check on the flocks of finches, pipits and ptarmigan feeding across the slopes. It needs an undisturbed cliff ledge and clear air below it, and nothing at all to build with — just loose gravel to scrape a hollow in.

requirements.hint: A high ledge with loose gravel on it and open sky underneath. Do not build a nest — a peregrine just kicks a dip in the grit.

records.name: Sand Dollar
records.diet: algae, plankton and scraps of food picked out of the sand grain by grain
records.shelter: Half buried on edge in rippled sand, in beds of hundreds at a time
records.preferredHabitat: Sheltered sandy bottoms just below the low tide line, where the current is gentle
records.fact: A living sand dollar is not white and smooth — it is purple and covered in tiny moving spines it uses to walk and to pass food along to its mouth. The white disc with the flower pattern is its skeleton, after everything else has washed away.
records.role: A whole bed of them stands half-buried on edge like coins in a slot, all leaning into the current to catch what drifts past. Where the water is rougher they lie flat instead so they do not get rolled away.

requirements.hint: Clean rippled sand just below the tide line, somewhere sheltered enough that the current is gentle.

records.name: Octopus
records.diet: shore crabs, clams, mussels, snails and shrimp, cracked open or drilled through
records.shelter: A crevice or empty shell it pulls a rock across behind itself, with a heap of emptied shells outside the door
records.preferredHabitat: Rocky subtidal seafloor and deep tidepools with plenty of crevices and cold, clean water
records.fact: An octopus has three hearts, blue blood, and tastes everything it touches with its arms — and because the only hard part of it is its beak, one the size of a dinner plate can squeeze through a hole the size of a grape.
records.role: The octopus is the top invertebrate hunter of the rocky shore, and the pile of emptied crab and clam shells outside its den is the easiest way to find one. It can change colour and skin texture in under a second to vanish against rock or kelp, despite being colourblind, and it will drill a neat hole through a stubborn clam and inject it to make the shell relax. Each octopus works through a huge number of crabs, which keeps the grazers and scavengers of the tidepools in check.

requirements.hint: Broken rock with gaps to hide in, and plenty of crabs. Leave the shell pile outside the den alone — that is how you know somebody is home.

sources.name: Monterey Bay Aquarium — East Pacific red octopus

records.name: Grizzly Bear
records.diet: roots, berries, ground squirrels, winter-killed carcasses — and moths, by the hundred thousand
records.shelter: Digs a den into a high slope in autumn and sleeps in it until the snow softens
records.preferredHabitat: Open high country with digging ground, berry slopes and no people
records.fact: Grizzlies climb above the trees in late summer to eat moths — flipping rocks to get at them and putting away up to 40,000 in a day, which is most of a year's fat in a few weeks.
records.role: The biggest thing on the mountain and the reason everything else stays alert. It digs up whole slopes hunting roots and ground squirrels, which turns the soil over, and it will drive a wolverine off a carcass without breaking stride.

requirements.hint: A high open slope soft enough to dig, rocks to flip, and a mountain already full enough to feed something this big.

records.name: Grasshopper Mouse
records.diet: scorpions, centipedes, beetles and other mice
records.shelter: Takes over a burrow another animal dug, then defends it
records.preferredHabitat: Open sandy flats with scattered brush and plenty of prey underfoot
records.fact: This mouse hunts scorpions, gets stung in the face, and carries on eating — its body turns the venom's pain signal off. Then it stands up on its hind legs and howls at the moon like a tiny wolf.
records.role: A mouse that decided to be a predator. It keeps scorpions and big insects in check, and it is one of the only animals that can eat the desert's most venomous residents without flinching.

requirements.hint: An old burrow it can take over and open ground to hunt across. It gets all its water from what it catches.

records.name: Snow Bunting
records.diet: seeds blown onto the snow, plus insects in the short summer
records.shelter: Deep in a rock crevice, lined with feathers and fur against the cold
records.preferredHabitat: Windswept ridges and fellfield where the snow blows clear
records.fact: Snow buntings nest further north than any other songbird on Earth, tucked so deep in rock cracks that the male has to feed the female in the dark while she sits.
records.role: A small bird that treats a blizzard as ordinary weather. Flocks drift across bare ridges picking up seed the wind has stranded on the snow, and they turn from white to warm brown as the season turns.

requirements.hint: A deep, dry crack in the rock out of the wind, and open stony ground nearby where the snow blows clear.

records.name: Groundhog
records.diet: grass, clover, dandelions and just about any tender green thing it can reach
records.shelter: A burrow with several entrances, a grass-lined sleeping chamber and a separate toilet room
records.preferredHabitat: Meadow edges with deep, well-drained soil it can tunnel through
records.fact: A groundhog digs a burrow with a front door, a back door, a bedroom and a separate room for going to the toilet — and moves about a tonne of soil doing it. In winter its heart slows to about five beats a minute.
records.role: The meadow's earthmover. Its abandoned burrows become homes for foxes, snakes, rabbits and half the small animals here, so one groundhog's digging outlives the groundhog by years.

requirements.hint: Deep, well-drained soil at the edge of the grass, with a bolt-hole close by. It wants somewhere to dig more than somewhere to hide.

records.name: Opossum
records.diet: almost anything — insects, fruit, eggs, carrion, and an enormous number of ticks
records.shelter: Sleeps the day out in a hollow log or a borrowed burrow, and rarely uses the same one twice
records.preferredHabitat: Brushy edges with hollow wood, water nearby and plenty to scavenge
records.fact: When an opossum plays dead it is not acting — it faints. The body goes stiff, the tongue lolls out and it gives off a smell like something long dead, and it cannot snap out of it for several minutes even if you walk away.
records.role: The meadow's clean-up crew. It eats what everything else has left, including carrion and vast quantities of ticks, and it is the only animal here that carries its young around on its back.

requirements.hint: Hollow wood to sleep the day away in and berries within a night's walk. It moves house constantly, so give it more than one option.

records.name: Song Sparrow
records.diet: insects and spiders in summer; seeds, berries and grass heads the rest of the year
records.shelter: A cup of grass tucked low in a shrub or a thick tussock, close to damp ground
records.preferredHabitat: Brushy, slightly damp edges — the messy strip between open grass and thicker cover
records.fact: Every song sparrow makes up its own tunes. A young male listens to the neighbours, then invents his own set of eight or ten and sings them for life, so you can learn to tell individual birds apart by ear.
records.role: One of the first birds to find a mending meadow and one of the last to leave it. It works the scruffy middle ground, eating insects all summer and switching to seeds in winter.

requirements.hint: A damp, messy corner with a thick tussock to hide a nest in and berries close by. they like the untidy bits best.
